Subject: Hosted API: sudden p99 regressions on long-context workloads

Hi Lauren / Redwood support,

We started seeing a sharp increase in p99 latency for our hosted API traffic this morning. The regression correlates with long-context calls (we use 16k and 32k window requests). Quick summary from our monitoring:
- baseline (last 30 days): p95 ~420ms, p99 ~1.2s for 16k workloads
- this morning (08:00–08:10 PT): p95 ~600ms, p99 spiking to 5.8s for 16k requests
- 32k requests are even worse: p95 ~1.1s, p99 ~10.4s
- error rate increased from 0.02% to 0.6% during the spike; tail timeouts observed (502 / 504)

We attached a short sample log (acme_p99_samples.log) with request IDs and timestamps. This is impacting two critical pipelines for our recommendations product; latency above p99 3s degrades SLAs to our customers.

Can you confirm whether there were any config rollouts or model changes this morning? Any guidance for short-term mitigation would be appreciated — we can shift traffic or apply client-side throttles if recommended.

Thanks,
Tanya Rios

Acme Analytics

Hi all — I'm Grace from Infra/Runtime reliability. I dug into our telemetry and here's what we see so far:

Summary of findings (first-pass):
- No control-plane rollout was pushed in the last 12 hours. No model weights have been changed for ACME's pinned model.
- We observed a sudden change in request-length distribution for ACME's tenant at ~07:45 PT: concurrent 32k-window calls increased by ~3.5x vs baseline.
- Our serving runtime's background memory pressure and KV cache churn increased significantly, leading to higher per-token CPU scheduling jitter and occasional request timeouts under sustained concurrency.

Immediate mitigations applied (now):
1) Route ACME traffic to a lower-latency compatible variant (quantized-8b) for 32k requests — reduces p99 by ~40% in our tests.
2) Enabled preferential KV prefix caching for ACME's top-50 keys to reduce repeated decoding cost.
3) Emergency concurrency cap for 32k-window calls to 6 concurrent requests per tenant while we stabilize.
4) Increased short-term worker pool size by +15% in the affected region to absorb bursts.

Attachments: hosted_p95_p99_trends.pdf (pre/post comparisons), mitigation_checklist.xlsx (operational steps and rollback plan).

Planned next steps and timeline:
- 0–2h: monitor pre/post metrics (we expect p99 to drop to <3s for 32k; p95 under 1.2s for 16k)
- 2–12h: if stable, gradually increase concurrency cap and shift a percentage of traffic back to the original variant for quality checks
- 24–72h: perform deeper root cause analysis (heap/KV eviction patterns) and prepare a permanent optimization (kernel scheduling tweak and model compile profile)

Needed from Acme: a 32k redacted request payload and a short-lived API key we can use to replay a sample in staging (we will not store the key). Also please confirm if you accept the temporary routing to quantized-8b.

—Grace
Grace O'Connor

Markus / Neha — quick executive summary from the ACME escalation:

1) Impact: ACME saw p99 for 32k requests spike to ~10s for ~15 minutes; error rate briefly rose to 0.6%. Business impact: two customer-facing pipelines degraded.
2) Cause (initial): burst of increased large-window concurrency causing KV cache churn and runtime memory pressure; no recent control-plane/model rollouts detected.
3) Immediate action taken: route to quantized-8b variant for 32k, enabled KV prefix caching, applied concurrency cap (6), increased worker pool +15%. Initial post-mitigation metrics look positive — p99 reduced to ~2.6s for 32k in staging tests.
4) Next 72h plan: staggered rollback after quality checks, permanent runtime scheduling/compile profile change, longer-term kernel selection improvement.
5) Commercial ask: Ben may propose a one-off credit for the covered SLA window.

Related artifacts: JIRA-INC-1127 (incident ticket), hosted_p95_p99_trends.pdf, mitigation_checklist.xlsx attached to the thread.

Recommend we authorize the temporary credit up to $12k if ACME requests it — Ben can confirm the exact amount. Also recommending an expedited post-mortem with the ACME engineering team early next week.

—Lauren
